newsitem.title: UK: BA warns time running out for American deal.
newsitem.headline: BA warns time running out for American deal.

text.p: British Airways Plc threatened Wednesday to abandon its proposed alliance with American Airlines and with it support for an Anglo-U.S. open skies aviation trade deal if regulatory approvals are not granted before November.

"It is really up to the authorities to decide whether they want consumers to enjoy the benefits of open skies and more competition at Heathrow (airport) that this deal will bring," a company spokesman said.

He was confirming remarks made by BA Chief Executive Robert Ayling in an interview with the Financial Times published Wednesday that he wanted the deal approved by November, when the world airline industry routinely meets to agree on allocations of runway slots at busy airports for next year's summer season, which starts in April.
"After that it becomes more difficult," Ayling said. "There comes a point in any transaction where not having approval is tantamout to being told 'No'."

"There are some key dates," company spokesman David Budgens said. "The November slot conference is one which we need to take into account in planning for the launch of the alliance. We cannot wait forever," he said.
But Budgens also pointed out that Ayling said in the interview that he was hopeful the regulatory process was picking up again after last month's election in Britain.

"Obviously while it is true that we have become frustrated at the time that it has taken to win approval, we want this deal done," the spokesman said. "There are signs of movement in Washington, Whitehall and in Brussels and we are still hopeful that the alliance can proceed," he added.

Ayling, Virgin Atlantic President Richard Branson, American's chairman Robert Crandall and others were scheduled to appear before the U.S. House of Representatives' aviation subcommittee Wednesday, but the session was postponed due to the pressure of full House business.
However, at a news conference, Branson accused Ayling of "breathtaking arrogance" for linking approval of the proposed alliance with support for an open skies agreeemnt.

"Who made Robert Ayling and Bob Crandall the arbiters of British and U.S. national aviation policy?" Branson asked. "With breathtaking arrogance, Mr. Ayling has said if they're not granted anti-trust immunity, there will be no open skies agreement between the United States and Great Britain."
Branson said American Airlines had made similar statements on its website.
It was exactly a year ago that BA and American announced the alliance. But they are still struggling to win approval in the United States and Europe in the face of fierce opposition.
Under the proposed alliance, BA intends to co-ordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

Rival airlines, the European Union's Competition Commissioner and consumer groups have all objected to the deal, alleging that it would dominate Europe's biggest trans-Atlantic market and lead to higher fares.
But BA and American say their deal would lead to greater competition, not less, because it would allow all U.S. airlines access to compete at Heathrow, Europe's most important transatlantic airport.

Both Britain and the United States have made approval of the alliance conditional on both sides agreeing to liberalise the transatlantic market with an open skies pact, which requires Britain to open up London Heathrow to greater competition.
Adding to the delays, EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert said last week that he did not expect the Commission to rule on the deal before September.
